titulo_es: Obligation and advice: must, have to, should
resumen: Must and have to express obligation (Spanish “tener que”); should gives advice (Spanish “debería”). In the negative their meaning changes a lot: mustn't forbids, don't have to shows that something is not necessary.

filas: obligation felt by the speaker, written rules
She has to wear a uniform.

explicacion.texto: Must and should are modal verbs: they do not take -s in the third person, they are followed by the infinitive without to and they do not use do in questions (Must I...? Should we...?). Have to is an ordinary verb: has to, do you have to?, didn't have to.
Must has no past or future form: for the past use had to (I had to work yesterday) and for the future will have to (You'll have to wait).

items: Mustn't ≠ don't have to: You mustn't tell him (it is forbidden) versus You don't have to tell him (it is not necessary, you decide).
Should suele suavizarse con I think: I think you should see a doctor.
To ask for advice: What should I do?

ejemplos.traduccion: Los pasajeros deben mostrar su billete.

ejemplos.frase: I have to get up at six every day.
ejemplos.traduccion: Tengo que levantarme a las seis todos los días.

ejemplos.frase: We don't have to pay; it's free.
ejemplos.traduccion: No tenemos que pagar; es gratis.

ejemplos.frase: Did you have to wait long?

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: You mustn't come if you are busy.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: You don't have to come if you are busy.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If something is not necessary, use don't have to; mustn't is a prohibition.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: You should to see a dentist.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Should is followed by the infinitive without to.

errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I had to work last weekend.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: In the past, use had to.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of have to.
ejercicios.frase: My sister ___ (have to) work on Saturdays.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that have to is an ordinary verb and is conjugated: in the third person singular it is has to. The clue is the subject My sister, which is equivalent to she. That is why the form is “has to work”. It is an external obligation, imposed by the work timetable, which is exactly the meaning the table gives to have to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hermana tiene que trabajar los sábados.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With a third person singular subject (my sister) you need has to.
The third person of have is irregular: has, not haves.
To is missing: the structure is has to + infinitive.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with mustn't or don't have to.
ejercicios.frase: You ___ park here. It's for ambulances only.
ejercicios.explicacion: The contrast on the card applies, “Mustn't ≠ don't have to”: mustn't expresses prohibition. The clue is the second sentence, “It's for ambulances only”, which shows that parking there is not allowed. That is why the answer is mustn't (or must not). Don't have to would say that it is not necessary to park, which makes no sense here.
ejercicios.traduccion: No puedes aparcar aquí. Es solo para ambulancias.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Don't have to means “it is not necessary”; here parking is forbidden, so you need mustn't.
Have to forms the negative with don't, not with haven't; and besides, a prohibition is needed here.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with mustn't or don't have to.
ejercicios.frase: Tomorrow is a holiday, so we ___ go to school.
ejercicios.explicacion: The same contrast applies: don't have to shows that something is not necessary. The clue is “Tomorrow is a holiday”: going to school is not forbidden, it is simply not necessary. That is why the answer is don't have to (or do not have to). Mustn't would mean that going to school is forbidden.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: It is not necessary: don't have to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mañana es fiesta, así que no tenemos que ir al colegio.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Mustn't expresses prohibition; a holiday does not forbid going, it only makes it unnecessary: don't have to.
The subject is we, so the form is don't, not doesn't.
Have to does not form the negative with haven't; you say don't have to.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the past form of have to.
ejercicios.frase: The flight was cancelled, so we ___ (have to) stay at a hotel.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that must has no past form and that for the past you use had to. The clue is “The flight was cancelled”, in the past, which means we are talking about a past obligation. The form is had to, the same for all persons. The result is “we had to stay at a hotel”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Obligation in the past: had to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cancelaron el vuelo, así que tuvimos que alojarnos en un hotel.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Must has no past form; past obligation is had to.
It is in the present; the sentence is about the past, so it is had to.
Have is irregular: its past is had, not haved.

ejercicios.frase: You look tired. You ___ go to bed so late.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines should / shouldn't as advice or opinion. The clues are “You look tired” and “so late”: going to bed so late is what causes the tiredness, so the advice is negative. That is why the form is shouldn't (or should not), followed by the infinitive without to.
ejercicios.traduccion: Pareces cansado. No deberías acostarte tan tarde.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Should would advise going to bed late, the opposite of what the context requires.
Mustn't expresses prohibition; here it is friendly advice, which is given with shouldn't.
Should is a modal verb and is followed by the infinitive without to.

ejercicios.frase: It's a great film. You ___ see it.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines should as advice or opinion. The clue is “It's a great film”: the speaker recommends seeing it. Should is the right option for a recommendation, followed by the infinitive without to. Mustn't would forbid it and don't have to would say it is not necessary.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es una película estupenda. Deberías verla.

por_opcion.should: Correct. Should expresses a recommendation: “you ought to see it”.
por_opcion.mustn't: Incorrect. Mustn't forbids seeing it, which contradicts it being a great film.
por_opcion.don't have to: Incorrect. Don't have to means “it isn't necessary for you to see it”, exactly the opposite of a recommendation.

ejercicios.frase: ___ wear a tie at your new job?
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that have to is an ordinary verb and forms questions with do: do you have to? The clue is that the question is about an external rule at work. That is why the form is “Do you have to wear a tie?”. Must does not take to and have to is not inverted like an auxiliary.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Have to forms questions with do.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿Tienes que llevar corbata en tu nuevo trabajo?

por_opcion.Must you to: Incorrect. Must is a modal verb and is followed by the infinitive without to; “Must you wear…?” would be possible but sounds formal, and here it has to.
por_opcion.Do you have to: Correct. Have to forms questions with do: Do you have to + infinitive.
por_opcion.Have you to: Incorrect. Have to is not inverted like an auxiliary; this form is old-fashioned and is not used in modern English.

ejercicios.frase: Next year he ___ pay more taxes.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that must has no future form and that for the future you use will have to. The clue is “Next year”, which places the obligation in the future. As will is already a modal verb, it cannot be followed by another modal like must; that is why have to is used: “he will have to pay”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Must has no future form: will have to.
ejercicios.traduccion: El año que viene tendrá que pagar más impuestos.

por_opcion.will must: Incorrect. Two modal verbs cannot go together; must has no future form.
por_opcion.will have to: Correct. Will have to is the future of obligation.
por_opcion.musts: Incorrect. Must is a modal verb and never takes -s; besides, it does not express the future.

ejercicios.frase: Visitors ___ feed the animals. It's dangerous.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines mustn't as prohibition. The clue is “It's dangerous”: it is a rule that forbids a behaviour, as on a sign at the zoo. Mustn't is the right option. Don't have to would say that it is not necessary and should would encourage doing it.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los visitantes no deben dar de comer a los animales. Es peligroso.

por_opcion.mustn't: Correct. Mustn't expresses prohibition, consistent with it being dangerous.
por_opcion.don't have to: Incorrect. Don't have to means “it is not necessary”; it does not forbid anything.
por_opcion.should: Incorrect. Should would advise feeding the animals, the opposite of what “It's dangerous” indicates.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the sentence into the past.
ejercicios.frase: I have to finish the report.
respuestas: I had to finish the report.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card states that the past of have to is had to, the same for all persons. The transformation consists only of changing have to had; the infinitive finish does not change. The result is “I had to finish the report”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The past of have to is had to.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Must has no past form; past obligation is had to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I had to finished the report.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After to comes the unchanged infinitive: finish.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have had to finish the report.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the present perfect (Spanish “he tenido que”); the task asks for the past simple: had to.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that should is a modal verb and does not take -s in the third person. The clue is shoulds, with an -s added by analogy with ordinary verbs (he stops). The correction is “He should stop smoking”. Remember that after stop the verb goes in the -ing form: stop smoking.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Should is a modal verb: no -s.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: should is a modal verb and does not take -s.
After a modal verb comes the infinitive without -s: stop.
Should is followed by the infinitive without to.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that must is a modal verb and is followed by the infinitive without to. The clue is “must to”, a mixture of must and have to. The correction is “We must leave now”. If you want to use to, you have to change the verb: “We have to leave now”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Must is followed by the infinitive without to.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: must does not take to.
Must is a modal verb and never takes -s; besides, the to mistake is still not corrected.
After must comes the infinitive, not the -ing form.

ejercicios.frase: Does she has to work tomorrow?
respuestas: Does she have to work tomorrow?
ejercicios.explicacion: The card explains that have to forms questions with do and that after does the verb is in the infinitive. The clue is “Does she has”: does already carries the third person marker, so have must not carry it. The correction is “Does she have to work tomorrow?”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: After does, have in the infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Does she has to work tomorrow?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: after does, have is in the infinitive.
Have to is not inverted like an auxiliary; questions are formed with do.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Do she have to work tomorrow?
errores_previstos.explicacion: With she the auxiliary is does, not do.

ejercicios.enunciado: Put the words in order to make a question.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes “What should I do?” as the way to ask for advice. As should is a modal verb, the question does not use do as an auxiliary: the order is question word (What), modal (should), subject (I) and infinitive (do). Here do is the main verb meaning “to do”, not an auxiliary.

errores_previstos.explicacion: That order only works in indirect questions (I don't know what I should do); in a direct question should goes before the subject.
Should is a modal verb and is not combined with do as an auxiliary.

respuestas: You don't have to take your shoes off
You don't have to take off your shoes
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines don't have to as “it is not necessary”. The order is subject (You), don't have to and the infinitive of the phrasal verb take off with its object your shoes. As take off is separable, the object can go between the two parts (take your shoes off) or after them (take off your shoes); that is why both are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Subject + don't have to + infinitive; take off can be separated.
ejercicios.traduccion: No hace falta que te quites los zapatos.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You have don't to take your shoes off
errores_previstos.explicacion: Don't goes before have: don't have to.

errores_previstos.respuesta: You don't have take to your shoes off
errores_previstos.explicacion: To goes immediately before the infinitive: have to take.

descripcion_larga_es: Must and have to express obligation (Spanish “tener que”) and should gives advice (Spanish “debería”). They are verbs in constant use for talking about rules, duties and recommendations. Spanish speakers find the negative especially difficult, because “no tener que” is translated in two very different ways: mustn't forbids and don't have to shows that something is not necessary. It is also hard to remember that must and should take no -s, no to and no do.

contexto.que_es: These are the basic forms for expressing obligation, prohibition, lack of necessity and advice. Must and should are modal verbs: they do not change with the person, they are followed by the infinitive without to and they form questions without do. Have to is an ordinary verb that is conjugated (has to, had to, will have to) and needs do in questions and negatives.
contexto.por_que_importa: They are used every day to explain rules, give instructions or give advice. Confusing mustn't with don't have to causes serious misunderstandings: saying “You mustn't come” forbids someone to come, when perhaps you only meant that it was not necessary. In A2 and B1 exams it is one of the most frequently tested contrasts.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They appear when talking about rules at work or in a place (You mustn't smoke here), about timetables and external obligations (She has to wear a uniform) and when giving advice (You should rest). Spanish speakers tend to translate “no tienes que” as mustn't every time, to put -s or to after must and should, and to use must for the past instead of had to.
